props.title: Kentucky Fried Movie
props.initialSlug: A wild comedy ride of outrageous movie spoofs

sections.content: Kentucky Fried Movie (1977) launched the careers of comedy titans Jim Abrahams, David Zucker, and Jerry Zucker before they created Airplane! (1980). This anarchic sketch comedy film pioneered the rapid-fire spoof format, throwing countless gags at the screen in a frenetic mix of movie parodies, fake commercials, and absurdist segments. The standout "A Fistful of Yen" section mercilessly lampoons Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon (1973) while perfectly capturing exploitation cinema's gleeful excess.

sections.content: The film's influence extends far beyond its modest budget and initial reception. Modern parody franchises like Scary Movie (2000) and Date Movie (2006) borrowed heavily from KFM's template of rapid-fire references and genre satire. The film's fearless approach to politically incorrect humor and willingness to break the fourth wall influenced everything from Monty Python's The Meaning of Life (1983) to Family Guy (1999-present).

What sets Kentucky Fried Movie apart is its commitment to recreating the exact look and feel of what it's parodying. The "Big Jim Slade" commercial segment nails the overwrought masculinity of 70s sports equipment ads, while "Catholic High School Girls in Trouble" perfectly mimics exploitation film trailers. This attention to detail would become a hallmark of the ZAZ team's later work in The Naked Gun (1988) and Hot Shots! (1991). SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Sketch Comedy Films

sections.content: While Kentucky Fried Movie wasn't the first sketch comedy film - The Groove Tube (1974) and Tunnel Vision (1976) came before - it perfected the format. Its influence can be seen in later works like Monty Python's The Meaning of Life (1983) and The Kentucky Fried Movie's spiritual successor Amazon Women on the Moon (1987). The film's mix of high and low humor, combined with its willingness to tackle any target, created a template that sketch comedy shows like Mr. Show (1995-1998) would later follow.
